SECTION I: Read the text and answer the subsections a), b) and c).

                    How a city feeds people and cuts waste




EH
Every day, hungry people arrive at India’s first Garbage Cafe in Ambikapur in the
hope of getting a hot meal. But they don’t pay for their food with money. Instead,
they hand over packs of plastic such as old carrier bags, food wrappers and water
bottles. There, people can trade a kilogram of plastic waste for a full meal that
includes rice, two vegetable curries, dal, roti, salad and pickles.

The Garbage Cafe was launched in 2019 using the slogan “more waste, better




  U
taste” and the purpose was simple: to encourage low-income people, especially
the homeless, to collect plastic waste from streets and landfills, and give them
hot meals in return.

Rashmi Mondal is a local woman who brings plastic to the cafe. Every morning,
she sets out early on the streets of Ambikapur in a search for abandoned plastic
and, for her, collecting such rubbish is a means of survival.

The cafe has also had an impact on the amount of plastic waste going to landfill.
Almost 23 tonnes of plastic have been collected in total since 2019, contributing
to a wider fall in the amount of plastic going to landfill from 5.4 tonnes per year to
2 tonnes in 2024.

The plastic collected in the Garbage Cafe is sent to specialised local waste
collection centres. Ambikapur now has 20 of these decentralised centres, which
sort collected waste into more than 60 categories. The centres employ 480

                    INGELESA                              INGLÉS
women called swachhata didis or “cleanliness sisters”, to do this waste
segregation as well as going door to door each day to collect household waste.

Staff at the waste collection centres are provided with gloves, masks and other
sanitary facilities to reduce health risks while handling waste. In contrast, those
collecting the waste on the streets are not provided with this hygiene support, so
they have to face daily exposure to bacteria, sharp objects and toxic waste
leading to a risk of illness.

However, such schemes have not always run smoothly. The city of Delhi also
launched a plastic waste collection initiative using garbage cafes, but the




EH
operation has slowly collapsed. The lower enthusiasm might be due to the fewer
people being on low incomes than in Ambikapur.

And while the plastic waste collection cafes have had an impact, they are not able
to tackle problems such as the overproduction of plastic, non-recyclable plastics
and lack of proper segregation in most Indian households. It is more like a quick
fix that deals with the surface issues rather than the root causes of the plastic




  U
problem.

Abridged and adapted from: Hazra Khatoon (2025, August 19). Rice, two curries and dal: The
Indian Cafes where you pay in rubbish. BBC.

SECTION I: Read the text and answer the subsections a), b) and c).

  My ‘Chinglish’ has a strong Australian accent – but I’m determined to
                             pass it on to my child

My seven-month-old daughter was lying on her play mat, holding her tiny feet in




             U
her hands. She looked exactly like she was doing the “happy baby” yoga pose. I
wanted to tell her this in Mandarin, but halfway through the sentence I realised I
didn’t know the Mandarin word for “yoga”. She smiled at me, waiting, and I had
to finish the sentence in English. This mix of simple Mandarin, English words and
my strong Australian accent is what I am passing on to her. When I read her
Chinese baby books, I often don’t know many of the words. It feels like we are




EH
learning together, step by step.

It’s strange that I am now trying to teach her Mandarin, because, when I was
young, I tried hard to hide my Chinese background. While growing up in Australia
in the 1980s and 90s, I spoke loudly in a clear Australian accent so that no one
would think I was “too Chinese”. At that time, it felt safer to distance myself from
my culture. My father had arrived from Malaysia in 1973, just as Australia was
moving away from the White Australia rule. He believed that fitting into
Anglo-Australian culture was necessary.

My parents worked hard and sent my siblings and me to good private schools.
There, I met girls who seemed to represent the “ideal” Australian image: tall,
confident country girls. I didn’t realise that my own story—children of immigrants
working for a better future—was also becoming part of Australia’s identity. My
parents tried to raise me bilingual. When I was about ten, they sent me to
Saturday Chinese school. But I felt embarrassed because younger children who
spoke Chinese at home were far ahead of me. I soon gave up.

                          INGELESA                                          INGLÉS

Nowadays, multiculturalism has gone from a government rule to a source of
national pride: the most recent Scalon Institute survey shows 85% agree
multiculturalism has been good for the country. Multilingualism is now seen as
both a personal and professional strength, creating opportunities to work
overseas and in globalised markets. Studies demonstrate its cognitive benefits:
boosting memory, problem-solving and mental flexibility, while also delaying
dementia.

Many second-generation parents like me want to pass on their languages, even




                   U
if imperfectly. A friend told me she had the same experience in Punjabi school;
however, she still plans to raise her baby bilingually. She reminded me that
parents simply do their best. Unlike my parents, I have more resources: bilingual
childcare, language apps and community programs. Sometimes I worry that my
Mandarin is too weak. But another colleague once shared how a single
Portuguese word from her childhood became a precious link to her culture. It




EH
made me realise that even small pieces of language matter.

Language is more than grammar and vocabulary; it’s a bridge through time. Even
when fractured and messy, it connects generations. One day, if my daughter
passes on even one awkward phrase of our “mixed Mandarin”, it will carry our
family’s story with it.

Abridged and adapted from: Monica Tan (2025, January 28). My ‘Chinglish’ has a cringe-inducing ocker accent – but I’m
determined to pass it on to my child. The Guardian.
